entities.summary:
Robert Pullen (died 1146-09-29), an English theologian and cardinal, emerged as a pivotal intellectual figure in the early 12th century, instrumental in shaping both the theological discourse of his era and the nascent institutional structures of higher learning in England. His career spanned from teaching in Paris to serving in the Roman Curia, bridging the burgeoning scholastic centers of Northern Europe with the ecclesiastical heart of the Catholic Church. Pullen's work contributed significantly to the systematization of Christian doctrine, influencing a generation of scholars who would later define the intellectual landscape of medieval universities.

Educated perhaps at Laon, Pullen rose to prominence as a master of theology in Paris, a hub of intellectual ferment during the 1130s. He is credited with introducing the *Sentences* as a teaching method, predating Peter Lombard's more famous compilation, thereby laying groundwork for scholastic methodology. In 1133, he returned to England, possibly teaching in Oxford, where his presence is often cited as a foundational moment for what would become Oxford University, though formal university structures were still decades away. Pope Innocent II summoned him to Rome around 1140, elevating him to Cardinal-Priest of Santi Silvestro e Martino ai Monti and later, in 1144, to Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church under Pope Lucius II, a position he held until his death.
